title: Principles ten to thirteen
hook: God knows, rewards and punishes, the messiah will come, the dead will live

segments.voice: Yesterday, principles six to nine, and your line: prophecy and Torah. Did you give one plain line the attention of a famous one? Today, the list's last stretch. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

Thirteen lines, and every one opens the same way. I believe with complete faith. That's the shape of a version of Maimonides' list printed in prayer books, set out after the morning service. It isn't his own wording. Someone later recast each foundation as a sentence a person could say in the first person, out loud. So the list stops being a page of philosophy and becomes something said with the mouth. Today, the last four lines, the ones that look ahead.
screen: `THIRTEEN LINES, ONE OPENING.` → `I BELIEVE WITH COMPLETE FAITH.` → `THE LINES THAT LOOK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Principles ten to thirteen. The tenth: God knows what human beings do and think. Not in a general way, from far off. The Psalms say God fashions the hearts of all people and considers all their deeds. Nothing a person does falls outside God's notice. The eleventh: God rewards those who keep the commandments and punishes those who break them. Maimonides holds that the final reward is the world to come, the share this whole list began with. The twelfth: the messiah will come. And here the prayer-book version adds a phrase. Even though he may delay, I wait for him every day that he will come. Not a date on a calendar. A waiting that starts over each morning. The thirteenth: the dead will live again, at a time God chooses. That's the resurrection of the dead, a belief already present in the Mishnah chapter Maimonides was explaining. Now look at the whole list from here. It began with God, who has no beginning. It passed through prophecy and the Torah. And it ends with things that haven't happened yet. A creed that closes on hope rather than on a fact already settled. Some Jews say these lines each morning. Others study them, and argue with them, which is tomorrow. Each line still opens the same way. I believe with complete faith.
screen: `GOD KNOWS WHAT PEOPLE DO.` · `REWARD AND PUNISHMENT.` · `WAITING FOR THE MESSIAH, EVERY DAY.` · `THE DEAD WILL LIVE.` · then, large: `I BELIEVE WITH COMPLETE FAITH.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hold one hope. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for: for yourself, for someone you love, or for the world. Not a plan. A hope. Notice how it sits in you. Is it tired? Is it bright? The twelfth line waits every day, without knowing the day. Try holding your hope that way for a few breaths, open, unhurried. If you pray, you can hold it before God. Then let it rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Principles ten to thirteen. God knows what people do, God rewards and punishes, the messiah will come, and the dead will live. Today's word.
Your line: I believe with complete faith. Today, once, notice something you're waiting for, and let the waiting start fresh instead of stale. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Some Jews recite the thirteen "I believe" lines, Ani Ma'amin, after the morning service; the twelfth line, about waiting for the messiah, is also sung to several melodies.

fork.setup: you're recasting Maimonides' list so people can say it aloud. how should each line begin?
fork.reveal: the prayer-book version opens every line with the same first-person words: I believe with complete faith.

original.note: Hebrew: I believe, the words that open each line of the prayer-book version of the list.

trapdoor: what you thought: four predictions about the end of the world.
what it means: God knows, rewards and punishes, the messiah will come, and the dead will live.
what a scholar hears: the list closing on hope, and the later Ani Ma'amin turning Maimonides' philosophy into first-person lines said aloud.

notes: 'I believe with complete faith' is the index carry and a translation of 'ani ma'amin be'emunah shelemah'; the Ani Ma'amin is cited as paraphrase since no public-domain translation is on the approved list.
Ani Ma'amin 'printed in prayer books, after the morning service' and 'isn't his own wording' (author unknown, later than Maimonides): please confirm.
Twelfth line paraphrased: 'even though he may delay, I wait for him every day that he will come.' Please confirm the rendering.

Psalm 33:15 paraphrased (fashions the hearts of all, considers all their deeds); Maimonides cites a verse for the tenth principle (some texts give Genesis 6:5 or Jeremiah 32:19); please confirm which.
'Maimonides holds the final reward is the world to come': from his discussion in Perek Chelek. Please confirm the phrasing.
'The resurrection of the dead, a belief already present in the Mishnah chapter' refers to Sanhedrin 10:1's exclusion of one who denies it. Please confirm.
howItsDone: 'sung to several melodies' stated generally; please confirm.
Editor pass: dropped the word count ('the same five words', true only of the English) from the hook.
